turns.doctor_question: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you. Could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Hey, Dr. Smith. Yeah, nice to meet you too. Well, I'm here because... man, I just don't know what to do with myself anymore. It’s like... you know when you leave a truck running in the driveway and you can just hear it idling out there? That’s me. I got this motor running inside me all day long. Just humming and vibrating, all the time. 

And if I have to just sit still somewhere—like, say, at church. I try to go and just sit in the pew like everybody else, but I can't do it. I feel like I'm literally trapped in that wooden seat. My skin starts crawling, my legs start bouncing, and I just have to get up or do something, mess with something, anything. Even at home, I can't just sit on the couch and relax. I'm up, I'm down, I'm pacing around the house. Same thing right out there in your waiting room at the clinic just now! I was about to wear a hole in your carpet out there because sitting in those little chairs just makes me feel boxed in, like a caged animal or something. I just always, always have to be moving or getting up to do something, and I can't figure out how to shut the motor off.

symptom_reasoning.S010: The patient explicitly mentions that their 'legs start bouncing' when they try to sit still.
symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient describes an inability to remain seated in situations where it is expected, such as at church or in the waiting room, stating they 'just have to get up'.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient reports intense feelings of restlessness, pacing around the house, and feeling 'trapped' or 'like a caged animal' when forced to sit.
symptom_reasoning.S014: The patient explicitly states they feel like they have a 'motor running inside me all day long' and cannot shut it off.

turns.doctor_question: Has this feeling of being constantly 'on the go' and unable to sit still been a part of your personality for as long as you can remember, or is this something that started more recently?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, man, no, this ain't a new thing at all. It's been my whole life, I swear. As far back as I can remember, I've had this exact same problem. 

I mean, you can go all the way back to when I was just a little boy in school. It was a complete disaster, honestly. The teachers... man, they were just at their wits' end with me every single year. They were always, and I mean *always*, moving my seat around the classroom. They’d put me right up front by the chalkboard so they could keep an eye on me, and then two days later they'd move me to the very back corner, then over by the window, then back to the front... just trying to find somewhere I wouldn't be a nuisance. But it didn't matter where they stuck me, because I just could not stay put. I'd be tipping my chair back, wandering over to the pencil sharpener, messing with the kid next to me. 

And it wasn't just the moving around, neither. I was always getting yelled at because I talked out of turn constantly. The teacher would be right in the middle of a lesson, and a thought would pop in my head and I'd just blurt it right out. I didn't even mean to be disrespectful, it just sort of flew out of my mouth before my brain could put the brakes on. 

And getting to the end of a lesson? Forget about it. I got in so much trouble for jumping up before class was even done. Like, the bell hadn't even rung, the teacher was still assigning homework or whatever, and I was already on my feet, practically halfway out the door. My legs just couldn't take being shoved under that little metal desk for one more second. It drove everybody crazy—my teachers, my folks. So, yeah, this motor... it's been running hot since day one. I don't think I've ever had a time in my life where I wasn't just bouncing out of my own skin like this.

symptom_reasoning.S010: The patient describes squirming and tipping his chair back while seated at his desk.
symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient explicitly states he would wander around the classroom and jump up out of his seat before class was dismissed.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient describes intense physical restlessness, noting his legs couldn't take sitting and feeling like he was 'bouncing out of his own skin.'
symptom_reasoning.S014: The patient confirms the feeling of being constantly on the go, stating his 'motor' has been 'running hot since day one.'
symptom_reasoning.S016: The patient admits to constantly blurting thoughts out during lessons before he could stop himself.

turns.doctor_question: Looking back at your time in school, along with all that moving around and blurting things out, did you also struggle with things like losing your homework, forgetting your supplies, or having a hard time focusing on tasks that didn't interest you?
turns.patient_response:
Well, see, the thing about focusing... it ain't even just about school or homework. I mean, sure, that stuff was hard, but it's more about just trying to pay attention when anybody is talking to me about anything that takes more than a minute or two to say. It's exactly like that right now, every single day. 

Like, when folks are talking through things... say my buddy is trying to figure out ride times so we can get somewhere, or somebody is rattling off a pantry list of what we need from the store, or even down at the church when they're going over the plans for the week or how they're gonna organize a potluck or whatever. I swear to you, Dr. Smith, I try so hard. I start out strong. I listen good at first, you know? I'm looking right at 'em, nodding my head, taking it in. 

But then... I don't even know how it happens, it's just like a switch gets flipped or the radio station just completely loses the signal. My mind just slips off. I'll start looking at the way the light hits the floor, or I'll hear a car drive by outside and wonder what kind of engine it's got, or my leg starts bouncing again, and the person is still standing right there moving their mouth, but I ain't processing a single word. 

And then they finish talking and look at me waiting for an answer, and I realize I just missed all the pieces I really needed to hear. The important stuff! Like what exact time I was supposed to be ready by the curb, or what specific kind of soup to get for the pantry. It drives folks absolutely crazy because they think I'm ignoring 'em on purpose, or they think I just don't care. And I try to explain, like, I was with you for the first sentence, I really was, but then I just drifted off into outer space. It's just exhausting, honestly, always having to ask people to repeat themselves because my brain just won't stay locked in on what folks are saying.

symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient describes a persistent inability to sustain attention during conversations that last more than a minute or two, noting their mind slips off.
symptom_reasoning.S003: The patient explicitly states they stop processing words when spoken to directly, causing others to think they are ignoring them on purpose.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient describes being easily distracted by extraneous stimuli, such as the way light hits the floor or the sound of a car driving by outside.
symptom_reasoning.S010: The patient mentions that their leg starts bouncing while trying to listen, indicating fidgeting behavior.

turns.doctor_question: When you look back at your life, would you say that the constant need to move and the blurting out of thoughts have been a bigger problem for you than the difficulty with staying focused and organized, or have both been equally difficult to manage?
turns.patient_response:
Man, that’s a tough one to weigh out. I mean, the bouncing around and the blurting stuff out, that gets me yelled at right to my face, you know? People get mad at me right then and there. But the other stuff... the staying organized part? That might actually be ruining my life just as bad, maybe even worse, just in a slower, quieter kind of way. 

Because, see, my stuff is just a complete and total disaster area. Like, I try to keep things straight, I really, really do. I tell myself, 'Okay, I'm gonna put all my important stuff right here on the kitchen counter so I know where it is.' But then... I don't know, it just explodes. My papers, the mail, those little appointment cards they hand you at the front desk—like the one for today, I practically had to tear my house apart looking for it this morning—it all just gets completely mixed up together. 

And it ain't just papers, neither! It's literally everything. Like, I'll bring in food boxes, maybe a box of macaroni or some stuff from the church pantry, and I set 'em down on that same counter. And then I start writing a note on my phone so I don't forget to call somebody back... and then my phone notes get just as cluttered as the physical counter! I got a hundred notes in that phone that just say random words I don't even understand anymore. 

So I end up with this giant jumbled pile of food boxes, loose papers, appointment cards, and a phone full of nonsense, and I just stand there staring at it all. I look at the mess and I literally cannot figure out what needs doing first. My brain just... it just locks up. Like, do I put the boxes in the cupboard? Do I read the appointment card? Do I try to decode the phone note? I can't pick a starting point to save my life. So you know what I do? I just walk away. I go pace the yard or mess with something in the garage because looking at it makes my head spin. 

And because I can't figure out how to just start, I don't do any of it. And then, by the time I finally get forced to deal with it, everything is already late or completely messed up. I miss the appointments, the bills get late fees, the food boxes get knocked over and spill everywhere... it's just a constant cycle of me making a mess and not knowing how to fix it until it's too late. So, yeah, I guess they're both pretty terrible in their own ways.
